summary: Describes Client Hints, a way for HTTP clients to proactively tell servers about their characteristics, such as device or network traits, using request header fields. This is an experimental approach to content negotiation that tries to balance performance against the privacy cost of sending extra information.

eli5.summary: Your browser tells a website a little about itself, like screen size, so the site can send the best version, but only when the site asks.

questions: how do servers request client information from browsers
how does the accept-ch header work
why is client hints better for privacy than passive fingerprinting
how do servers and browsers negotiate client hints
subtitle: Enabling servers to explicitly request client characteristics without passive fingerprinting

tldr.problem: Servers want to optimize content for different devices (mobile vs. desktop, slow network vs. fast), but sending that information passively in every request fingerprints users and wastes bandwidth. User-Agent detection and cookies are inflexible and not portable.
tldr.mechanism: Client Hints is a framework where servers explicitly opt-in to receiving specific client characteristics via a new Accept-CH response header, and browsers send those headers only when the server has asked for them, turning passive fingerprinting into active, visible opt-in.
tldr.outcome: Servers can request exactly the hints they need, browsers send only what servers ask for, and the explicit opt-in enables users and researchers to see which sites collect what information about them.

facts.label: Persistence
facts.value: Session duration; cleared on data clear

today: RFC 8942 is Experimental with IETF consensus and is used on the web today. Browsers support the Accept-CH opt-in mechanism, and servers use Client Hints for responsive content delivery. The framework is designed to be extensible, allowing new hints to be defined in follow-on specifications without changing this RFC.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Web applications run on thousands of different devices with varying screen sizes, network speeds, and capabilities. Traditionally, servers have tried to optimize content delivery by detecting the browser type (via User-Agent matching), using HTTP cookies, or encoding preferences in URLs. None of these approaches work well.

User-Agent detection requires maintaining a database of device signatures, is unreliable, cannot infer dynamic user preferences, and relies on passive fingerprinting. Cookies require JavaScript execution on the client, are not portable across applications, and are not cache-friendly. URL parameters must be repeated on every link and suffer from lack of portability.

Client Hints offers a better approach grounded in proactive content negotiation: browsers send specific request headers that servers have explicitly asked for, allowing servers to select an appropriate response. This framework:

  • Reduces request size bloat by only sending headers that will actually be used.
  • Protects privacy by requiring explicit server opt-in; browsers reveal information only to servers that ask, and users and researchers can audit which sites are requesting what.
  • Is portable: the same hints can be understood by any server.

The tradeoff is that information must still be sent to the server as a request header; the Client Hints mechanism does not eliminate that sharing, but makes it transparent and opt-in.
sections.eli5: Websites used to spy on your browser by looking at what it says about itself all the time. Client Hints say: websites can ask what they want to know, and your browser only tells them if they ask, so you can see who is asking for what.

sections.title: How Client Hints Work
sections.content:
Client Hints are request headers that browsers send to convey information about the user's environment, device, or preferences. Examples include screen width, network type, or user agent details. Each hint is a separate HTTP header field.

Sending hints is controlled by default settings, user configuration, and an explicit server opt-in. Browsers SHOULD require opt-in for hints that expose high-entropy information (revealing; could identify individual users). Low-entropy hints (coarse and widely shared, like major browser type) can be sent without opt-in, though browsers vary in their interpretation.

The opt-in mechanism is the Accept-CH response header. When a server sends Accept-CH: Sec-CH-Width, Sec-CH-DPR in a response over HTTPS, it tells the browser: "I want to receive the width and device pixel ratio headers on subsequent requests." The browser persists this preference, bound to that origin, for the session duration and sends the named headers in future same-origin requests.

Important scope rules: The opt-in is bound to the origin (e.g., "https://site.example"), not the full hostname. Hints are sent on same-origin navigation and resource requests (e.g., "https://site.example/image.jpg") but not to other origins or subdomains ("https://thirdparty.example" does not receive the opt-in). If a user clears site data, cookies, or cache, persisted opt-in preferences are cleared.
sections.eli5: The website sends back a message saying, "Tell me your screen width and how many dots per inch." The browser remembers that for that website and sends those headers in the next request. If the website does not ask, the browser does not send.

sections.title: Hint Headers and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC itself does not define specific hint headers. Instead, it establishes the framework and guidelines; individual hints are defined in separate specifications (e.g., User-Agent Client Hints in [UA-CH]).

Naming convention: Client Hint headers are encouraged to use a CH- prefix to make them identifiable (e.g., CH-Foo) or a Sec-CH- prefix to prevent JavaScript from setting them (ensuring the browser, not page scripts, generated the value). The Sec- prefix protects against script injection and signals that the header represents genuine browser characteristics.

Accept-CH format: The Accept-CH response header is a Structured Header (RFC 8941) whose value is a list of tokens, one per hint the server wants to receive. For example: Accept-CH: Sec-CH-User-Agent, Sec-CH-Viewport-Width

Cache interaction: When a server varies its response based on one or more Client Hints, it MUST include a Vary response header naming those hints. This tells caches that the response key depends on those header values. For example, Vary: Sec-CH-Width, Sec-CH-DPR indicates that the same URL might serve different responses to clients with different screen widths or pixel densities, so caches must key on both.
sections.eli5: Headers usually start with "Sec-CH-" so the browser knows it made them, not a website script. When a server sends different pages depending on screen size, it also says "this answer varies by screen size" so caches know not to mix them up.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Information exposure: Client Hints headers reveal information about the user's device and preferences. This information is equivalent (from a security perspective) to what JavaScript APIs can access; Client Hints merely expose it as headers. However, uncontrolled active fingerprinting (with explicit server opt-in) is not automatically better than passive fingerprinting (no opt-in).

Entropy and linkability: High-entropy hints (very specific values) can be combined across requests to link users to an identity. Implementations SHOULD reduce entropy by restricting header values to coarse ranges. For example, instead of exact screen width, a hint might report width ranges ("small", "medium", "large") so many devices report the same value.

Sensitivity: Hints MUST NOT expose user-sensitive information that is gated behind user actions (like geolocation permissions). They also SHOULD NOT expose information that changes frequently unless the change is visible to JavaScript (e.g., battery level should not be a hint unless the page can observe it).

Preventing abuse: Servers should only opt-in to hints they actually use. The Accept-CH header itself is not hidden; implementations SHOULD monitor access to Client Hints like access to JavaScript APIs. Users and researchers can audit which origins request which hints by examining Accept-CH responses.

Scope and delegation: Hints are sent only to the origin that requested them, not to third parties. Additional mechanisms (outside this RFC) can allow an origin to delegate hint access to third parties on its behalf, with user consent.
sections.eli5: Sending hints exposes information. Browsers can limit the detail (like saying "small screen" instead of the exact number). Servers should only ask for hints they actually use. You can see which sites are asking by looking at their responses.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 8942 is an Experimental specification with IETF consensus. It was produced by the Internet Engineering Task Force and approved by the IESG.

The Accept-CH response header and the Client Hints concept are in use on the web. Examples of Client Hint headers defined elsewhere include User-Agent Client Hints (for detailed browser, OS, and platform information), viewport width and device pixel ratio (for responsive design), and Save-Data (a signal that the user prefers to use less bandwidth). Browsers including Chrome, Edge, and others support the framework and the Accept-CH opt-in mechanism.

The framework is designed to be extensible: new hint headers can be registered without changing this specification. Each new hint should follow the privacy and security guidelines laid out in Section 4 of this RFC.
sections.eli5: This is an experimental way of doing things that is now being used by real websites. Different browsers are adding support for it. New kinds of hints can be added as needed.
